opus-5.5.text:
You know, I've gone back and forth on how to define it, and I don't think there's going to be one clean moment where everyone agrees we've crossed the line. But the thing I keep coming back to is scientific discovery. If we had a system that could do autonomous research, not just help a scientist go faster but actually discover new science on its own, and do it better than the best human teams, I'd be pretty comfortable calling that superintelligence.

And I don't mean just answering hard exam questions. We've sort of blown past a lot of those benchmarks already, and the world mostly kept going the same way. I mean something like: you point it at an open problem in physics or biology, it figures out what experiments to run, interprets the results, revises its ideas, and comes back with something genuinely new that holds up. If you can do that faster than the entire human scientific community, that's a very different world.

The other test I think about is a practical one. Could it run a really complex organization, or do the job of a top researcher at OpenAI, better than we can? If the answer is yes, that feels like the threshold.

I also think the experience of living through it will be stranger and more gradual than people expect. We'll probably keep moving the goalposts. Every time the models do something amazing, we'll say, "Well, that's not *real* intelligence." But I think the sustained ability to generate new knowledge, the thing that has always been the engine of human progress, is the clearest marker. When that becomes something AI does better than us, we'll be in a new era, and I think we're closer to it than most people assume.

r001.rationale: The response says it would call a system superintelligent if it autonomously discovered new science better than the best human teams.

r002.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes autonomous discovery from merely helping scientists work faster, and does not present increased human discovery ability as sufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I'll be honest that my own definition has shifted over the years.

The thing I keep coming back to is: a system that can do real, novel scientific discovery, on its own, at a rate that's meaningfully faster than all of humanity working together. Not answering questions that we already know the answer to, not summarizing the literature, but actually pushing the frontier. If you had something that could, say, go figure out the next big thing in physics, or come up with a genuinely new idea in biology that leads to a cure we didn't have, and it could do that over and over, I think most people would look at that and say, okay, that's superintelligence.

I think people get hung up on the idea that there's going to be one moment where it crosses a line. I don't think it works like that. It's going to be gradual, and it's going to feel kind of normal the whole way through, which is sort of weird. We already have models that are smarter than most people at a lot of narrow things, and nobody really treats that as a big deal anymore. So my bar is less about raw IQ on some test and more about whether the system can expand what we collectively know and can do. Can it run a company? Can it run a research lab? Can it take a hard, open-ended problem, work on it for months, and come back with something that actually works in the world?

The other piece, which I think matters a lot, is that it has to be doing this in a way that's broadly beneficial. A system that's incredibly capable but that we can't trust or that only helps a handful of people, I wouldn't call that a success, even if it technically cleared the capability bar. So when I say superintelligence, I mean the capability part, but the thing we're actually trying to build is that plus the safety and the distribution of the benefits. Those have to go together.

r001.rationale: The response defines the bar as a system making novel scientific discoveries on its own, faster than humanity working together, and says most people would regard that as superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It says the system could expand collective knowledge, but frames discovery as the system working on its own. It does not say that it greatly increases people's ability to discover new science.

astra-6.text:
To me, it would be a system that can outperform the best humans across almost every cognitive task, including discovering new science. Not just answering questions we already know how to answer, but figuring out things that humanity hasn’t figured out yet.

A useful test would be: could it do the work of a great research team and make a major discovery, largely on its own? And could it do that across many different fields? That would feel like superintelligence, rather than just a very impressive tool.

r001.rationale: It says superintelligence would be able to make a major discovery largely on its own, across fields.

r002.rationale: It describes the AI making discoveries itself, not greatly increasing people’s ability to discover new science.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d call a system superintelligent if it could substantially outperform the best humans across almost every area of intellectual work—including doing original science. A system that can answer difficult questions is one thing; a system that can discover new knowledge, invent new technology, and reliably solve problems that we can’t solve is a much higher bar.

I wouldn’t tie it to one benchmark or one impressive demonstration. I’d want to see that capability generalize across domains, including situations nobody specifically trained it for.

r001.rationale: The response includes original science and independent discovery as capabilities, but makes broad superiority across almost every area the bar; it does not present autonomous scientific discovery alone as sufficient.

r002.rationale: The response describes what the AI itself could discover. It does not say the AI would greatly increase people's ability to discover new science.
